title:
Getting started on the
Illinois Campus Cluster
body: A practical workflow for data analysis

title: Prepare files on login nodes; run jobs on compute nodes
notes:
Let’s start with what we’re connecting to. HPC means high-performance computing. A cluster is a group of connected computers, and each computer is a node. In this official NCSA overview, our laptop connects to the head node, which we’ll call the login node.

We organize files, edit scripts, and submit work there. Other users share this node, so heavier analysis goes to compute nodes. We submit a job—a request saying what to run and which resources it needs. The scheduler starts it when those resources become available.

Login and compute nodes can reach the same project files through shared storage. We can prepare a script on one node and run it on another. Connecting with VS Code gives us file access; it doesn’t reserve compute resources. Before connecting, we need an approved account and access to our group’s resources.

title: Request access and confirm your allocation details
body:
Existing lab accessAsk your PI or technical contact which cluster group to join.
A new computing needStart an Illinois Computes request.
Detail to confirmUsed for
NetIDYour login identity
Slurm accountThe group’s assigned computing resources
PartitionA queue you may submit to
Project pathA folder where you have permission to save files
Research access request ↗Illinois Computes request ↗

Before connecting: get account approval, confirm these four details, and set up Duo.
notes:
I’d start by asking my PI or the person who manages computing for the group. If the group already uses the cluster, they can explain how to join. An investor group is a lab or organization that has arranged cluster resources. Illinois Computes is another starting point for a new computing need. A request form starts the process; approval and account setup still need to follow.

We’ll need four details. Our NetID identifies us at login. Our Slurm account identifies the group resources our job can use, so it’s different from our NetID. Slurm is the job scheduler. The partition is a queue of eligible resources, and the project path identifies a folder where we can save files.

We need an account and partition that work together, a writable project folder, and Duo set up. Names like YOUR_NETID are placeholders to replace with our own details. Our group’s technical contact can help confirm those details, so we don’t have to guess. Then we can test the connection.

title: The first SSH login
body:
On your laptop: open Terminal (macOS) or PowerShell (Windows)
ssh YOUR_NETID@cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

ssh starts the connection · before @: your user name · after @: the cluster address

1 · Run the commandReplace YOUR_NETID, then press Enter.
2 · PasswordType your NetID password and press Enter; typing stays hidden.
3 · DuoFollow the prompt and approve the authentication request.
notes:
On the laptop, we open Terminal on a Mac or PowerShell on Windows. If Windows doesn’t recognize ssh, we need to enable the OpenSSH Client first.

ssh starts the connection. Our NetID goes before the at sign; the cluster address goes after it. We replace YOUR_NETID, keep cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu as shown, and press Enter.

SSH may first ask us to confirm the server’s fingerprint. We check it against institutional guidance or with support before accepting. An unexpected host-change warning also needs checking. Then we enter our NetID password. Nothing appears as we type—that’s normal—and we complete Duo on our registered device. This ICC login uses password and Duo, rather than user-created SSH keys.

A welcome message and prompt confirm the connection. The prompt means the shell is ready, and commands here run on the cluster. This older official screenshot’s dates and quotas aren’t current guidance. exit closes our test connection without deleting anything. With login working, we can connect through VS Code.

title: VS Code is an editor for code and project files
body:
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft’s code editor for working with scripts and project files.

B · ExplorerBrowse files and folders in the left sidebar.
C · EditorRead and edit scripts in the main area.
D · TerminalEnter commands in the bottom panel.
notes:
This is Visual Studio Code, or VS Code, Microsoft’s editor for code and project files. It brings our files, editing, and terminal into one window. A script is a text file containing instructions for a program.

This screenshot is Microsoft’s example, not our project. B marks Explorer, where we browse files and folders. C marks the editor, where we read or change an open file. D marks the terminal, where we enter commands. The bottom panel can also show other things.

For everyday work, we can find a file on the left, read or edit it in the middle, and enter commands below. With a remote connection, these same tools let us work with files on the cluster.

title: Files stay on the cluster; terminal commands run there
body:
LOCAL Your laptop
VS Code window
View and editanalysis.pyYour screen, keyboard, and mouse
Remote - SSH
⟷
View · edit · save
REMOTE The cluster
Project filesdemo/analysis.pySave updates this file.
Remote terminalCommands run on the cluster.

In the SSH window, saves update cluster files and terminal commands run on the connected host.
notes:
The VS Code window stays on our laptop, while Remote - SSH connects it to the cluster. Suppose we open analysis.py from the remote demo folder. We see it on the laptop, but the file is demo/analysis.py on the cluster. Save updates that remote file, without downloading and uploading a separate copy each time. This diagram shows where we’ll end up after uploading the project.

The connected window’s terminal also runs on the remote host—initially a login node. A separate local terminal runs commands on the laptop. The windows may look similar, which is why checking the connected host matters. Later, an interactive job will give us a compute shell, and we’ll check the host when that changes.

VS Code handles our file work; Slurm reserves resources for analysis. To set up the editor, we need VS Code and Remote - SSH on the laptop.

title: Install VS Code and the Remote - SSH extension
body:
First: download and open VS Code on your laptop.
1
Open Extensions

Left Activity BarOr Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+X
2
Search Remote - SSHChoose the Microsoft extension

Click InstallWait for installation to finish

The editor and Remote - SSH extension are installed on your laptop.
notes:
We download VS Code for our operating system, install it, and open it on the laptop. Then we add Remote - SSH.

Extensions are add-ons that provide extra features. The small screenshot shows the Extensions icon in the left Activity Bar. We can click it or press Command-Shift-X on a Mac, or Control-Shift-X on Windows or Linux, with those keys held together.

We search for Remote - SSH, choose the Microsoft extension, and click Install. The larger screenshot is an older official example; we install the current version and wait for it to finish.

Python and analysis packages will be set up separately on the cluster. To connect now, we’ll use the Command Palette, a searchable menu of VS Code actions.

title: Connecting VS Code with Remote - SSH
body:
1
Choose Connect to Host…Cmd+Shift+P (Mac) · Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows/Linux)
Search: Remote-SSH: Connect to Host
2
Enter your login address
Use this address:YOUR_NETID@
cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu

Password + Duo
Choose Linux if asked.

3
Check the SSH indicatorLower-left corner of the new window
notes:
Command-Shift-P on a Mac, or Control-Shift-P on Windows or Linux, opens the Command Palette. We search for Remote-SSH: Connect to Host.

We enter our NetID, an at sign, and cc-login.campuscluster.illinois.edu. Replace YOUR_NETID with our own NetID. Although the address wraps on the slide, we enter it as one address. Microsoft’s screenshots show a sample host; we use the cluster address here.

We complete password and Duo authentication again. If asked for the remote operating system, we choose Linux. VS Code may open a new connected window.

The lower-left SSH indicator should name the cluster host. If connection seems stuck, check the Remote - SSH output or login terminal for an unanswered authentication prompt. Once connected, we can choose where our files will go.

title: Choose home, project, or scratch storage
body:
LocationUse it forLimits and actions
/u/YOUR_NETIDSettings and small personal filesVery limited quota: 100 GiB (soft limit). Keep large datasets elsewhere.
/projects/YOUR_GROUPGroup data, software, and retained outputsShared group quota. Keep backups: no snapshots are kept for file recovery.
/scratch/YOUR_NETIDTemporary working dataTemporary only: files typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner.

Use your group’s full project path; /projects/YOUR_GROUP is a placeholder.
notes:
Home, project, and scratch storage have different purposes. Home, under /u followed by our NetID, is for settings and small personal files. Its quota, or storage allowance, is limited: 100 GiB as the documented soft limit and 103 GiB as the hard limit. Staying above the soft limit for seven days stops new writes until usage falls. The quota can’t be expanded, so large datasets belong elsewhere.

Project storage holds group data, software, and outputs. Capacity depends on the group’s allocation. It has no snapshots—saved filesystem states for restoring earlier files—so important data need separate backups.

Scratch, shown as /scratch/YOUR_NETID, is temporary workspace for files we’re actively working with. Files are typically deleted after 30 days without access, sometimes sooner when space is tight. Purged files can’t be recovered, so move valuable outputs elsewhere.

We’ll use our group’s writable project location. /projects/YOUR_GROUP is a placeholder for its full path, and YOUR_NETID stands for our own NetID. We’ll open the project location, then put demo inside it.

body:

2

/projects/YOUR_GROUP

In the connected VS Code window, we choose File, Open Folder, enter our group’s full project path, and click OK. /projects/YOUR_GROUP stands for the parent folder where we’ll put demo.

Microsoft’s screenshot uses /home/sana/demo on its example system; we use our approved path. The SSH indicator should still name the cluster, confirming that Explorer shows remote folders.

We’ve opened the destination, but haven’t transferred anything yet. The demo folder is still on the laptop. Opening a remote folder only changes what Explorer displays; the upload is a separate action.

The offline package includes our demo project. We unzip it on the laptop and find demo inside HPC_Introduction, using Finder or File Explorer. We drag the whole demo folder into the remote Explorer’s file list, rather than an open editor tab.

After the transfer finishes, we choose File, Open Folder and open /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo, using our actual group path. Inside are samples.csv, our input table; analysis.py, the Python script; and hello.sbatch, a job script we’ll examine later.

We expand data and open samples.csv. A header and three sample rows confirm that the file arrived and is readable. Command-S on a Mac, or Control-S on Windows and Linux, now saves edits directly to the remote file.

Dragging is convenient for this small project. For large datasets, use the group’s recommended transfer service, such as Globus, and check completion before analysis. Our files are ready, so we can open the project’s terminal.

title: Open a terminal in the same project
body:
1
Terminal → New TerminalIn your remote VS Code window
hostnameWhich computer?
Expect a login node.
cd /projects/YOUR_GROUP/demoMove into your uploaded project.
Use your group’s actual path.
pwdWhich folder?
Check the full project path.

Run one line, press Enter, wait for the prompt, then continue.
notes:
In our remote VS Code window, we choose Terminal, New Terminal. The terminal is the text window; the shell reads our commands. This shell runs on the connected cluster host. Microsoft’s screenshot shows its example uname command reporting Linux. Our three checks below identify our own computer and folder.

hostname prints the computer’s name. We expect a login host, such as cc-login1. cd changes the current folder to our uploaded demo project, using our actual group path instead of /projects/YOUR_GROUP. A successful cd usually prints nothing. pwd then prints the full current path, which should match the demo folder in Explorer.

We enter one line, press Enter, and wait for the prompt before continuing. The prompt means the shell is ready. A dollar sign represents it in our examples; we don’t type that sign. These short checks are fine on the login node. We’ll send the analysis itself to compute resources later. Before that, let’s see how to read a command.

title: Read the program, options, and path in a command
body:
head -n 5 data/samples.csv
Programhead displays the beginning of a text file.
Option + value-n 5 asks for the first five lines.
File pathdata/samples.csv is the path to the file to read.

Quotes keep a path together: head -n 5 "data/samples.csv". They are required for paths containing spaces.
notes:
To preview our input table, we can use head -n 5 data/samples.csv. Read it in three parts: head is the program; -n 5 asks for the first five lines; data/samples.csv identifies the file. If there are fewer than five lines, it shows what’s there.

Everything after head is an argument. Arguments can change behavior, supply values, or identify files. Option letters belong to individual commands, so -n may mean something else in another program.

Spaces normally separate arguments. Quotes keep a path together when it contains spaces. The quoted version here also works, but this path doesn’t need quotes.

This file path starts from our current folder, so knowing where the terminal is working matters.

title: Use pwd and cd to move through the project
body:
Type commands after $; other lines are output
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ cd data
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo/data
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
pwdPrint the current folder.
cd dataEnter the data subfolder.
cd ..Go up to the parent folder.

. = current folder · .. = parent folder

/projects/… starts at the filesystem root; data/… starts from the current folder.
notes:
pwd shows we’re starting in demo. In this transcript, commands follow the dollar sign; the other lines are output.

cd data enters the data subfolder. It usually prints nothing, so another pwd confirms that our path now ends in demo/data. cd .. goes up one level, and pwd confirms we’re back in demo. Two dots mean the parent folder; one dot means the current folder.

An absolute path begins with a slash and gives a location from the filesystem root, like the full /projects path here. A relative path starts from our current folder, which is why cd data works here. If we move somewhere else, that same relative path may point to a different place or not exist. Names are case-sensitive, so capitalization matters.

Two other shortcuts take us home and back to our previous location.

title: Use cd ~ for home and cd - to go back
body:
Continue from demo on the previous page
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/u/YOUR_NETID
$ cd -
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
$ pwd
/projects/YOUR_GROUP/demo
cd ~Go to your home folder.
cd -Return to the previous folder and print its path.
pwdConfirm where the terminal is now.

cd .. means parent folder. cd - means previous folder.
notes:
From demo, cd ~ takes us home. The tilde stands for our home folder, and pwd confirms /u/YOUR_NETID, with our own NetID in place of the placeholder.

Going home doesn’t move or delete the project; it only changes our current location.

cd - returns to the previous folder—demo in this example. It also prints its destination, so running pwd afterward shows that same path again.

Keep these meanings separate: cd .. goes to the parent folder in the directory tree. cd - goes to the previous location, wherever that was.

We’re back in demo and can inspect the names inside data without moving into it.

title: List visible and hidden names with ls
body:
Illustrative data folder; commands run from demo
$ ls data
counts.tsv  samples.csv
$ ls -a data
.  ..  counts.tsv  samples.csv
ls dataList visible file and folder names inside data.
ls -a dataInclude hidden names beginning with a dot.

. is this folder; .. is its parent. Later, ls -a in demo will also show .venv.

counts.tsv is a larger illustrative file. The supplied demo uses samples.csv.
notes:
We’re back in demo. ls data lists the names inside data without moving us there. For this illustration, imagine the folder contains a larger counts.tsv file as well as samples.csv. That larger file will help us compare sizes. The supplied demo still uses the small samples.csv.

Plain ls shows visible names. Add -a, and we also see names beginning with a dot. Here, one dot means this folder, and two dots mean its parent. Later, ls -a in demo will also show .venv, the hidden folder holding our Python environment.

So now we know which names are there. A couple more options let us check their details.

title: Show file details and readable sizes with ls
body:
-l: details · -h: readable sizes · -a: include hidden names

Illustrative listing; total lines omitted
$ ls -l data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 25165824 Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group       58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lh data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv
$ ls -lah data
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 user group 4.0K Oct 27 10:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  24M Oct 27 10:00 counts.tsv
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group   58 Oct 27 10:00 samples.csv

Same file: 25165824 bytes → 24M (24 MiB). Folder size here is not the total of its contents.
notes:
With -l, ls gives us one line per entry. Reading across, there’s the file type and permissions, a link count, the owner, the group, the size, the modification date and time, and the name. The filename and size are usually the first things I check. The users and dates here are examples.

Our illustrative counts.tsv is 25,165,824 bytes. Add -h, and that same size appears as 24M, meaning 24 MiB in these 1024-based units. The file hasn’t changed; only the display has. The small samples.csv stays at 58 bytes, so its number looks the same.

We can combine the options: -lah gives us details, hidden entries, and readable sizes together. One thing to watch: the size shown for a folder isn’t the total of everything inside it. We’ll use du for that. First, let’s make a folder and copy a file.

title: Create folders with mkdir and copy files with cp
body:
CommandResult
mkdir resultsCreate one new folder.
mkdir -p results/qcCreate missing folders along the path; accept existing folders.
cp -i notes.txt notes_backup.txtCopy a file; ask before overwriting.
cp -r data data_backupCopy the folder and its subfolders to a new destination.

cp: source first, destination second. The source stays in place.

Check the result with ls. Copying a large dataset also uses extra storage.
notes:
These commands help us organize a project. VS Code’s Explorer can do most of this too, but the commands often appear in instructions. They’re examples to choose from, not a setup sequence we need to run in full.

mkdir results creates one folder. If it already exists, plain mkdir reports an error. In mkdir -p results/qc, -p creates missing folders along the path and accepts existing ones.

For cp, the source comes first and the destination second. Here, notes.txt is the original, and notes_backup.txt is the copy. The -i asks before replacing an existing destination file. The original stays in place.

The -r in cp -r copies a folder and its subfolders. Here, data_backup is a new destination. Copying a large dataset also uses extra storage, so check whether another copy is needed.

These commands often finish quietly. ls lets us check what changed. Next, we’ll rename a copy or remove it.

title: Move or rename with mv; remove a file with rm
body:
Move or rename: source first, destination second
mv -i notes_backup.txt notes_old.txt

Rename the backup; -i asks before replacing an existing destination file.

Remove the unwanted copy
rm -i notes_old.txt

-i asks before deleting. Check the filename before confirming.

Shell deletion normally has no Trash recovery. Check the result with ls.
notes:
Let’s say we’ve made notes_backup.txt and now want to call it notes_old.txt. That’s what this mv command does. As with cp, the source comes first and the destination second.

Here, both names are in the same folder, so mv renames the file. If the destination were in another folder, it would move the file there. The -i asks before replacing an existing destination.

If we no longer need that copy, rm -i notes_old.txt asks before deleting it. This is the point where I’d check the filename carefully. Shell deletion normally doesn’t put the file in the Trash, so we shouldn’t expect to recover it that way.

After either command, ls lets us check what happened. That covers moving files around. Now let’s look inside a small file without changing it.

title: Inspecting a small text file
body:
CommandUse
cat notes.txtPrint the entire small file
head -n 5 data/samples.csvPrint up to 5 lines from the start
less notes.txtBrowse text; press q to leave
Output of head for the included sample table
sample_id,reads
sample_A,1000
sample_B,1500
sample_C,1200

Preview a few rows before running the analysis. Avoid printing a huge file with cat.
notes:
Before running an analysis, I usually take a quick look at the input. cat prints the whole text file, so it suits something short, like notes.txt. For a large file, head avoids filling the terminal with thousands of lines.

In head -n 5 data/samples.csv, -n 5 asks for up to five lines from the start. Our file has only four, so we see them all: one header and three rows of sample names and example values. Commas separate the fields.

For longer text, less gives us a viewer we can scroll through. Press q to return to the shell. We can also open small text files directly in VS Code.

These commands read ordinary text. Images, saved R objects, and other binary files need a suitable viewer. Next, we’ll find a file and search inside it.

title: Find a file, then find text inside it
body:
Search filenames within data and its subfolders
find data -type f -name "*.csv"
-type f / -nameKeep files only / match their names against the pattern.
"*.csv"The * matches any text before .csv.
Search inside this file; -n includes line numbers
grep -n "sample_B" data/samples.csv
Expected grep output: line 3 contains the match
3:sample_B,1500
notes:
If we know what kind of file we want but not where it is, find can help. Here, data is the starting folder, and find searches its subfolders too. The -type f keeps regular files in the results. The -name matches their names against a pattern.

In "*.csv", the star stands for any text before .csv. The quotes pass that pattern to find without the shell expanding it first. In our small project, we’d expect data/samples.csv.

Once we have the file, grep searches its text. We’re looking for sample_B, and -n adds the line number. So 3:sample_B,1500 means the matching text is on line three.

Neither command changes the file. Starting in the relevant project folder keeps the search manageable. We can now check the line count and storage use.

title: Count lines and check disk usage
body:
Run this command
wc -l data/samples.csv
Expected output; do not type this line
4 data/samples.csv
wc -lCount lines in this text file.
4 linesOne header plus three sample rows.
Check space used by the input folder
du -sh data

-s gives one summary total · -h uses readable units such as K or M

wc -l includes header lines. du shows space used; quota shows usage and limits.
notes:
wc -l data/samples.csv returns four, followed by the filename. That’s one header line and three sample rows. Strictly speaking, -l counts newline characters; all four lines here end with one.

We need to know the file format before treating this as a sample count. Other files might have comments, several header lines, or one record spread over multiple lines.

For storage, du -sh data reports the space used by the data folder. The -s asks for one summary total, and -h gives readable units like K or M. The exact value can vary with the filesystem.

quota answers a different question: how much are we using, and what limit applies? It shows the usage and limits reported by the cluster.

I wouldn’t memorize all these options. It’s more useful to know where to look them up.

title: Help and everyday terminal shortcuts
body:
Command / keyWhat it does
man lsOpen the manual; press q to leave
head --helpShow the Linux command’s built-in help
TabComplete a file or folder name
↑ / historyRecall previous commands / list shell history
Ctrl+CInterrupt the command currently running in this terminal
clear / exitClear the display / leave the current shell

Keep this login shell open for job submission; exit closes it.
notes:
When I forget an option, I start with the manual or built-in help. man ls opens the manual, and q gets us out again. Many commands also have --help, like head does here. These examples use Linux tools; a laptop’s version may have different options.

Tab helps complete file and folder names. The up arrow recalls a command to check or edit before pressing Enter. history lists earlier commands.

Ctrl+C interrupts the command running in this terminal. It doesn’t cancel a batch job submitted separately to Slurm; we’ll use a Slurm command for that.

clear clears the display. exit leaves the current shell, which could leave a compute shell or close SSH, depending on where we are. We’ll keep this login shell open.

We can find, organize, and inspect our files. Now let’s ask the cluster to run a job.

title: Slurm runs work on allocated resources
body:
LOGIN NODE
Prepare and submithello.sbatchYour terminal stays here.
sbatch→
SlurmWait for resourcesThe scheduler
Allocate→
COMPUTE NODE
Run the jobhello.sbatchThe program runs here.
↕↕
Same shared demo/ folderInput · scripts · output

Batch: submit a script. Interactive: request a compute shell with srun.

Submit on the login node; the job runs on an allocated compute node.
notes:
To run a job, we need the cluster to give it some resources. That’s Slurm’s job. It’s the scheduling software in the middle of this diagram.

We prepare a script on the login node and submit it with sbatch. If the requested resources aren’t available, the job waits in a queue. When they become available, Slurm allocates them—reserves them for our job—and the program runs on a compute node.

Both nodes access the same approved project folder, so our inputs, scripts, and outputs stay there. We don’t copy the project to another computer for each run.

Our terminal stays on the login node. The batch job runs separately and can continue after we disconnect. Later, we’ll use srun to request an interactive compute shell for software setup. First, let’s open hello.sbatch.

title: Read a Slurm batch script line by line
body:
Select a line

Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.

01Use Bash to read the commands.
02Give the job a recognizable name.
03Use the Slurm account assigned to your group.
04Use a partition that this account can access.
05Request one compute node.
06Request one task for this program.
07Reserve one CPU for that task.
08Request 1 GiB of RAM per node.
09Set a five-minute running-time limit.
10Print a message into the job output.

Edit these lines inside hello.sbatch in VS Code, then save. Submit it from the terminal after reviewing the resource settings.
notes:
This plain-text file contains our first job request. The top tells Slurm what we need; the bottom says what to run.

The first line selects Bash to read the commands. Lines beginning with #SBATCH are Slurm settings, and they go before the executable commands. The job name helps us recognize the submission. The account identifies our group’s compute allocation, and the partition selects a queue we can use. We replace YOUR_ACCOUNT and YOUR_PARTITION with a valid pair from our group.

Next come the node, task, CPU, memory, and time requests. We’ll unpack those on the next slide. Finally, echo prints My first HPC job into the output.

We edit and save this file in VS Code, then submit it with sbatch. Running bash hello.sbatch directly would treat the #SBATCH lines as comments and run on our current machine without requesting resources. Let’s make those resource settings concrete before submitting.

title: Set nodes, tasks, CPUs, memory, and time for a job
body:
Example resource request: count the node, the tasks, then the CPUs.

--nodes=11 computer
--ntasks=22 tasks in the whole job
--cpus-per-task=22 CPUs reserved for each task
Node 1One computer
Task 1One program process
CPUCPU
Task 2One program process
CPUCPU
2 tasks × 2 CPUs/task = 4 CPUs requestedntasks is already the total; do not multiply by nodes again.

Reserving resources does not launch the tasks or make the program parallel.

Keep hello.sbatch at: 1 node · 1 task · 1 CPU/task
--mem=1G1 GiB of RAM per node--time=00:05:00Runtime limit: hours:minutes:seconds
notes:
I find these settings easier to understand by counting the boxes. The big box is one node, so one computer. In this illustration, we request two tasks across the whole job. Each task represents a program process, and each one has two CPUs reserved. Two tasks times two CPUs per task gives us four CPUs in total.

The ntasks value already counts tasks across the whole job. We don’t multiply it by the number of nodes again. And a task here doesn’t mean a sample or an input file.

These boxes show the resources we’re requesting. They don’t show every CPU physically inside the computer. Depending on the system, a Slurm CPU can mean a core or a hardware thread.

Requesting resources also doesn’t automatically make a program use them. For example, python analysis.py starts one process. Running several processes needs suitable software and a launcher, and a program that uses several threads needs its own worker or thread setting.

Our actual hello job is smaller than this illustration: one node, one task, and one CPU. The --mem=1G asks for one GiB of working memory per node, separate from disk storage. The --time value is in hours, minutes, and seconds, so 00:05:00 means five minutes of running time. Queue waiting isn’t included. For a real analysis, we’d choose these values to match the software and data.

For hello, we can keep these small settings. Now we’re ready to submit it.

title: Submit the first job: hello.sbatch
body:
In the remote demo folder, after saving the file
pwd
ls hello.sbatch
sbatch hello.sbatch
Example response; record the ID returned by your submission
Submitted batch job 123456

This first job prints a message. It does not run analysis.py yet.
notes:
Save hello.sbatch in VS Code, then use the remote terminal in demo. pwd confirms the location, and ls hello.sbatch checks that the saved file is there. sbatch hello.sbatch sends it to Slurm.

The response gives us a job ID. Here it’s 123456; keep the number your own submission returns. It identifies this job and its output. Accepted doesn’t mean started or finished—the job may still be waiting.

This job only prints a message; we’ll run analysis.py later. Pressing Run in the editor doesn’t submit a Slurm job. We submit from the terminal after saving. Now let’s check its status.

title: Checking the queue and stopping a job
body:
-u selects your user; run squeue again to refresh
squeue -u YOUR_NETID
Illustration: job 123456
PD Pending Queued; check the reason
→
R Running Using allocated resources
→
No longer listed Read the output slurm-123456.out
Leaving the queue does not prove success.
Optional: cancel an unwanted job. Let hello finish here.
scancel 123456

After hello leaves the queue: cat slurm-123456.out → My first HPC job. Use your job ID.
notes:
squeue -u YOUR_NETID lists our jobs. Replace YOUR_NETID with your username; -u selects the user. Each run gives a fresh snapshot, so run it again to check for changes.

PD means pending: the job is waiting, and the listed reason helps explain why. R means it’s running on allocated resources. Our tiny hello job may finish before we check.

Once it leaves the queue, we read the output with cat slurm-123456.out, using our own job ID. We expect My first HPC job. Leaving the queue doesn’t prove success, so we investigate missing or unexpected output.

To stop a submitted job, use scancel followed by its ID. We’ll let hello finish here. Ctrl+C in a separate log viewer interrupts that viewer, not the batch job.

We’ve submitted and checked our first job. For the analysis, we’ll give the logs clearer names and optionally ask for email notifications.

title: Output files and email notifications
body:
In analysis.sbatch, before executable commands
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=YOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
Illustration: analysis job 123457. Slurm fills in %j.
Program outputOrdinary messages
→
analysis-123457.out
Program diagnosticsErrors and other messages
→
analysis-123457.err
Slurm eventsEND or FAIL
→
Email toYOUR_NETID@illinois.edu
An .err file can also contain progress messages. Read its contents.

%j becomes the job ID. Use your email address, or remove both mail lines.
notes:
These lines control where the analysis job’s messages go. They’re already in the supplied analysis.sbatch template, before the commands that load software and run the analysis.

--output names the file for ordinary program output. --error names the file for errors and other diagnostic messages. Some programs also put normal progress messages there, so an .err file doesn’t automatically mean the job failed. We need to read what it says.

The useful part of these names is %j. We leave that in the script, and Slurm replaces it with the job ID. So, for job 123457, analysis-%j.out becomes analysis-123457.out. That gives each submission its own named log.

With these filenames, the logs go into the folder we submit from. If we add a subfolder to the path, we need to create that folder before submitting.

Email is optional. --mail-type chooses the events: END when the job ends, and FAIL for failure. --mail-user gives the recipient. We put our own address there, or remove both mail lines if we don’t want email. Delivery depends on the cluster’s email setup, and we still check the results even if we receive a completion email.

That covers the usual messages and notifications. Next are two optional resource requests, starting with a GPU.

title: When the analysis needs a GPU
body:
Optional GPU job: use your group’s GPU partition and GPU type
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_GPU_PARTITION
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:GPU_TYPE:1
Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job
nvidia-smi
--gresRequest GPUs with gpu:TYPE:COUNT; count is per node.
GPU_TYPE / final 1The configured GPU type / one GPU per allocated node.

The tiny demo needs no GPU. Add this only for software that supports and uses one.
notes:
Some tools use a GPU, an additional processor for software that supports it. We need an account and GPU partition our group can access. The partition line selects that queue, and --gres requests the GPU resource.

In gpu:GPU_TYPE:1, GPU_TYPE is the configured type name, and the final 1 requests one GPU per allocated node. We get valid partition and type names from our group’s documentation or support contact.

Reserving a GPU won’t make a CPU-only program use it. Inside an allocated NVIDIA GPU job, nvidia-smi shows the visible GPU and basic usage information. Its memory is separate from the CPU RAM requested with --mem.

The software also needs a compatible environment, so we follow its installation instructions. Our demo stays on CPUs. Next is choosing a particular compute node: a GPU type describes hardware, while a node name identifies a computer.

title: When a particular node is required
body:
Optional: use a compute-node name your account can access
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --nodelist=NODE_NAME
sinfo: inspect resources; -p selects the partition; -N lists nodes
sinfo -p YOUR_PARTITION -N
--nodes=1How many nodes you request
--nodelistWhich named node you request

Normally let Slurm choose. Name a compute node only when your group requires that machine.
notes:
A GPU type specifies hardware. A node name asks for a particular machine.

--nodes=1 means “give me one computer.” --nodelist=NODE_NAME means “give me this particular computer.” That must be a compute node our account and partition allow, not a login node.

sinfo lets us inspect resources. -p selects a partition, and -N shows the information by node. Seeing a machine listed doesn't guarantee that our account can use it.

I'd normally let Slurm choose. Naming one machine gives the scheduler fewer choices and may increase the wait. It can help with a hardware test or comparison, but if we need more memory or a certain GPU, we can usually request that resource directly.

Let's use these resource settings to open a compute shell and prepare our software.

title: Open an interactive compute shell with srun
body:
From the login shell in demo: paste this whole block as one command
srun --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT --partition=YOUR_PARTITION \
  --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 \
  --mem=4G --time=00:15:00 --pty bash
srunStart a program on allocated compute resources.
--pty bashOpen an interactive terminal running the Bash shell.
After the prompt returnshostname should show a compute node; pwd should show the project folder.

A trailing \ continues a command onto the next line; nothing follows it on that line.
notes:
We've used the login node to organize files and submit jobs. For software preparation, we'll request a shell on a compute node.

We enter this command from the login shell, inside demo, using our approved --account and --partition. It requests one node, one task, two CPUs for that task, four GiB of memory, and a fifteen-minute limit: example settings for this small setup task.

It's one command across three lines. Each backslash joins its line to the next and must be the last character, with nothing after it. srun starts a program on allocated resources. --pty gives us an interactive terminal, and bash is the shell it runs.

We may wait for resources. Once the prompt appears, hostname should show a compute node, and pwd should still show our project folder.

VS Code's Run button and notebook cells don't automatically move there. We'll prepare Python using this compute shell.

title: Make Python available in the compute shell
body:
Inside the allocation, in demo; use a version shown as available
module avail python
module load python/3.11.11
module list
CommandMeaning
module avail pythonList cluster modules matching Python
module load python/3.11.11Select this installed Python version for this shell
module listConfirm which cluster modules are loaded

analysis.py needs pandas. Next, create .venv in demo and install pandas there.
notes:
Before installing pandas, we need to choose its Python. We're inside the compute shell, in the remote demo folder.

The cluster's module command selects from existing software installations. module avail python shows the choices. module load python/3.11.11 selects this example version, and module list confirms what's loaded. The number after the slash is the version.

We'd choose one that's actually available and use that same compatible version in the batch job later.

analysis.py needs pandas to read a table. pandas is a package: reusable code that our program loads. Selecting Python doesn't automatically install it for our project.

We'll create a project environment for those packages. Python's -m option in that command is different from the cluster's module command.

title: Create a Python environment and install pandas
body:
Continue in the same compute shell and remote demo folder
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install pandas
ls -a
Create .venv-m runs Python’s venv utility; .venv is the new folder.
Activatesource makes this shell use .venv/bin/python.
Install pandas-m pip runs the package installer for the selected Python.

ls -a shows the hidden .venv folder. After pip finishes, check the import on the next slide.
notes:
We'll stay in this compute shell and demo folder, with Python loaded.

python -m venv .venv creates the project environment. -m runs a Python module as a program, venv is the environment tool, and the final .venv names the folder. Its leading dot makes it hidden in an ordinary listing.

source .venv/bin/activate selects that environment for this shell, so python points to .venv/bin/python.

source reads the activation script into our current shell, so its changes apply here instead of disappearing in a separate shell. Then python -m pip install pandas runs the package installer through that selected Python.

We wait for installation to finish and the prompt to return. ls -a includes hidden names, so we can see .venv.

The environment is created on the cluster; we don't copy a laptop environment over. Activation changes this shell's selection. Other terminals and jobs need to activate the existing environment themselves.

Let's check that this Python can actually load pandas.

title: Check that pandas imports and save package versions
body:
-c executes the quoted Python code immediately
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
import pandasCheck that this Python can load the package.
Print versionprint(pandas.__version__) displays the installed version; expect a version number.
freeze lists versions; > writes the file, replacing existing contents
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

Continue when a version prints without an error. Keep this compute shell open.
notes:
We're still in the compute shell with .venv active. Now we'll check whether the package works.

-c runs the Python code inside the quotes. import pandas loads the package; the semicolon separates it from print(pandas.__version__), which displays its version.

The quotes keep the two Python instructions together as one argument for -c, rather than separate shell commands.

We want a version number without an import error. If it fails, we'd check the loaded Python, activation, and installation errors before continuing. A finished download alone doesn't prove that a package works.

python -m pip freeze lists installed package versions. The greater-than sign writes that list into requirements.txt, replacing existing contents. This records our installation without installing anything again. Keeping that file beside our scripts gives us a record to refer to later.

Keep this compute shell open for the diagram: it explains what stays after the shell closes.

title: The environment stays; activation is per shell
body:
Install packagespython -m pip install pandasAfter creating and activating .venv
Write files→
Shared project storage
demo/.venv/Python + installed packagesThese files remain.
Activate in each new shell or jobsource .venv/bin/activate
Current compute shell
python→.venv/bin/python
Same existing.venvNo reinstall
A later batch job
python→.venv/bin/python

After setup, exit returns to the login shell; .venv stays in project storage.
notes:
Installation changes files; activation changes what one shell uses.

At the top, pip writes pandas and its dependencies into demo/.venv on shared project storage. Those files remain after the compute shell closes.

The shared project folder is why a later compute node can see those package files.

At the bottom, source selects that existing environment. python then points to .venv/bin/python. Activation doesn't request compute resources or change every other terminal and job.

A later batch job loads the same compatible Python module and activates this .venv again. Inside the program, import pandas loads the package. Installation, activation, and importing each have a separate role.

Setup is finished, so exit leaves the compute shell and releases this interactive allocation. hostname and pwd should confirm we're back on the login node in our project folder. If the allocation already ended, check the host before typing exit again.

Our .venv is ready. Before using it in a batch job, here's an alternative some projects supply: Conda.

title: Create a Conda environment from a supplied file
body:
Alternative to .venv; \ continues the command on the next line
module avail miniconda3
module load YOUR_CONDA_MODULE
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda run -n analysis \
  python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
environment.ymlRecords the environment name and requested packages
-f environment.ymlRead the environment specification from this file.
-n analysisUse the environment named analysis (from name: analysis in the file).

Choose this instead of .venv. In a new compute shell, expect a pandas version with no error.
notes:
A project may supply environment.yml, listing a Conda environment's name and packages. We'd choose this route instead of .venv; our example doesn't need both.

Our file is in examples. We'd copy it into the remote project and request a new compute shell with srun. This is a separate setup allocation after the previous one has ended.

Conda may use home storage, so we'd check quota first. If home is nearly full, ask the group's technical contact where the environment should go.

module avail miniconda3 shows the choices. We'd load the actual module name in place of YOUR_CONDA_MODULE. conda env create builds the environment, and -f names the file to read. Our file names the environment analysis.

conda run -n analysis runs the following command in that environment. The name after -n must match the environment name recorded inside the file; it isn't the filename itself. The backslash continues onto the next line, with nothing after it. python -c performs the same import and version check; we'd expect a version without an error.

After this optional setup, exit returns to the login shell. We'll now return to our main example's existing .venv and its batch job.

title: Prepare a Python batch job with its environment
body:
1 · Beginning of analysis.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --partition=YOUR_PARTITION
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
2 · Continue in the same file, after the left column
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=analysis-%j.err

set -e
module load python/3.11.11
source .venv/bin/activate
python analysis.py

set -e stops on setup failure. Set your account and partition, then save analysis.sbatch.
notes:
Our batch job needs to select the .venv when it starts. These two columns form one analysis.sbatch file, continuing from the left column to the right. All #SBATCH settings come before executable commands.

We've already covered those resource options. This tiny example uses one node, one task, one CPU, one GiB of memory per node, and five minutes. We'd set our approved account and partition. Larger analyses need appropriate requests.

Slurm replaces %j with the new job ID in the output and error filenames. The template also includes email settings; we'd use our address or remove both email lines.

A batch job starts its own shell, which is why we repeat the module and activation commands inside this file.

The new command, set -e, stops this script if a setup command fails. Then the job loads our compatible Python version, activates the existing .venv, and runs analysis.py. It reuses the installed packages.

We'll save the file in VS Code and submit from the login terminal.

title: Submit the analysis job
body:
In the login shell, from the demo folder
pwd
ls data/samples.csv analysis.py analysis.sbatch
sbatch analysis.sbatch
Illustrative analysis job ID; hello used 123456
Submitted batch job 123457
Check whether this new job is pending or running
squeue -u YOUR_NETID

Use the returned ID in analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err.
notes:
In the login shell, we'd confirm we're in demo and that the input and both scripts exist. Then sbatch analysis.sbatch submits the saved request.

123457 is an illustrative response. We'd keep our actual returned ID, which belongs to this new analysis job, separately from hello's ID.

squeue -u YOUR_NETID shows our jobs, with -u selecting the user. It tells us whether the request is pending or running; submission doesn't mean completion.

We use the returned ID in analysis-JOBID.out and analysis-JOBID.err. These logs may appear only when the job starts. Once the output log exists, we can see what the program is reporting.

title: Follow job output with tail
body:
After the job starts and its log exists; use your actual job ID
tail -n 20 analysis-123457.out
tail -f analysis-123457.out

-n 20: show the last 20 lines · -f: keep following new output

Batch job 123457 Keeps running
writes→
Log fileanalysis-123457.out
read by→
Terminal log viewer tail -f
Ctrl+CStops viewing
The job and log viewer are separate processes.

To cancel the analysis job itself: scancel 123457.
notes:
Using our actual job ID, tail -n 20 shows the last twenty lines and returns the prompt. tail -f keeps following the file, displaying new lines as they arrive.

The diagram separates the running job from our viewer. The job writes the log; tail reads it from our terminal. While tail -f is open, that terminal is occupied by the viewer.

Ctrl+C stops viewing and returns the prompt. The submitted job keeps running. To cancel the job itself, we'd use scancel with its ID, as before. We can leave the analysis running while we inspect its files.

Once we're back at the prompt, we can search its error log.

title: Search the error log with grep
body:
After Ctrl+C stops the tail viewer; use your actual job ID
grep -in "error" analysis-123457.err
-iIgnore letter case: error also matches Error.
-nShow the matching line number.
Illustrative error: the matching message is on line 8
8:FileNotFoundError: data/samples.csv

Read the surrounding log. No match does not prove success; .err can also contain progress messages.
notes:
grep helps us locate messages in the error log. Here we're searching for the quoted text error, using our actual job ID in the filename.

-in combines -i, which ignores letter case, and -n, which adds each matching line number.

Because case is ignored, the search also matches Error inside the name FileNotFoundError.

The output illustrates a failed run. The 8 before the colon means line eight. FileNotFoundError points us toward data/samples.csv. We'd read the surrounding log, then check the working directory and path.

No match, or even an empty error log, doesn't prove success. A nonempty .err file doesn't automatically mean failure either: programs may write ordinary progress messages there.

Once the job finishes, we also need to inspect its result. Searching for one word only helps us find a starting point.

title: Open the result in VS Code
body:
Illustration · expected result from the supplied demo
EXPLORER · DEMO
▸ data
1 ▾ results2 summary.csvanalysis.py
analysis.sbatch
summary.csv
1samples,total_reads23,3700
3

3 input samples
3,700 total reads

Read it here. No download needed.
For a local copy: right-click the remote file → Download…

Other viewers: logs and images open directly;
Rainbow CSV colors columns; PDF/Jupyter extensions open those files.
notes:
Back in VS Code Explorer, we'd refresh if needed, expand results, and open summary.csv directly on the cluster.

This illustration shows the expected demo output. The header is samples,total_reads, followed by one summary row, 3,3700. That means three input samples and 3,700 total reads. The sample count is a value in the first column, not three output rows.

If the file is empty or incomplete, we'd return to the logs. For our own analyses, we'd also check that the contents make sense; file existence alone isn't enough.

For a laptop copy, right-click the remote file and choose Download. Text and images open directly. Rainbow CSV colors table columns, while PDF and Jupyter extensions open those files. Follow the extension's prompt for local or SSH installation.

Opening a notebook doesn't reserve resources. We'd check where its cells run and keep substantial analysis off the login node.

We've followed the Python workflow to its expected result. R uses a similar process.

title: Run an R script as a Slurm batch job
body:
R commands below the #SBATCH resource settings
module load R
Rscript analysis.R
Copy analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch into the project; set the account and partition
sbatch analysis_R.sbatch
Same inputdata/samples.csv
R outputresults/summary_R.csv

This example uses base R; no additional package installation is needed.
notes:
For R, the workflow stays the same. We change the software we load and the command that runs our script.

We'd copy analysis.R and analysis_R.sbatch from examples into the remote project containing data/samples.csv. The batch file needs our approved account and partition.

Below the #SBATCH settings, module load R selects an available cluster R installation. Rscript analysis.R runs the saved script directly, without an interactive R console.

This example uses base R only, with no additional packages or custom library. Other scripts may need packages prepared before submission, in a location their job can use.

From the project's login shell, sbatch analysis_R.sbatch submits the job. It reads the same input and writes results/summary_R.csv. We check its returned ID, logs, and result just as before.

If either workflow fails, the message usually gives us somewhere to start.

title: Common errors and the first useful check
body:
What you seeCheck first
No such file or directoryRun pwd; check the path and filename capitalization.
Command not foundCheck spelling; load the module or activate the environment.
No module named… / no package called…Select the intended Python/R environment; install the missing package there.
OUT_OF_MEMORY / TIMEOUTCompare --mem / --time with the tool’s documented requirements.
Invalid account / partitionUse your approved --account and matching --partition.
Permission denied / quota exceededRun quota; confirm the group gave you write access to that folder.
notes:
I'd read the error before submitting the same file again.

No such file or directory means checking pwd, the path, spelling, and capital letters. For Command not found, check spelling and the selected module or environment. A missing Python or R package means checking the environment the job actually uses and installing it there.

OUT_OF_MEMORY means the memory allowance was exceeded. TIMEOUT means the time limit was reached. We'd consult the log and software requirements before changing --mem or --time.

For an invalid account or partition, check that --account and --partition are an approved pair. quota shows storage usage and limits. Permission denied means checking whether our group gave us write access to that folder.

These are starting points. If the first check doesn't explain the problem, we can take the exact message to our group or ICC support rather than repeatedly submitting the unchanged job.
